title: GDPR Article 22 + EU AI Act: automated decisions done right
linkedinPost:
The EU AI Act's high-risk requirements went live on 2 August 2026. If your system makes automated decisions about individuals — credit scoring, fraud flagging, KYC — it is now subject to GDPR Article 22 AND the AI Act simultaneously.

Most legal teams are treating these as two separate compliance tracks. They are not. A single non-compliant automated decision system can draw enforcement under both.

The SCHUFA ruling (CJEU, December 2023) already confirmed: if the algorithm is determinative, a human reviewer in the loop does not save you from Article 22. Token review is not human oversight.

What I would actually do:

→ Map every automated output that affects individuals (credit, fraud, onboarding, pricing)
→ Run the Dual Trigger Test: does it produce significant effects? Is it Annex III high-risk? Both = full dual compliance obligation
→ Design human review that is genuinely independent — log the override rate. Under 1% is a SCHUFA risk
→ Build an Article 86 explanation record for every decision — I do this in n8n
→ Run the Dual Trigger audit annually. Model drift changes scope over time

The fintech operators who solve this now will not be the ones with the cleanest compliance decks. They will be the ones whose AI decisions are genuinely explainable, contestable, and independently reviewed.

That is not a compliance advantage. It is a revenue-per-employee one — because defensible decisions do not need to be reworked, re-reviewed, or reversed at scale.

Full piece + the Dual Trigger Test I use in every compliance design conversation — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between GDPR Article 22 and the EU AI Act for automated decisions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Article 22 gives individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects, and requires a legal basis plus human review. The EU AI Act adds risk classification, transparency obligations, and an explicit right to explanation (Article 86) for high-risk systems. Both apply in parallel — compliance with one does not satisfy the other.

mainEntity.name: Does a human reviewer always satisfy GDPR Article 22 requirements?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The CJEU's SCHUFA ruling (December 2023) confirmed that human review must involve genuine independent judgment. If the reviewer consistently accepts the algorithmic output without meaningful evaluation, the system is still 'solely automated' under Article 22 — regardless of the human step in the workflow.

mainEntity.name: Which AI systems are high-risk under the EU AI Act for financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: The EU AI Act's Annex III includes AI used in credit scoring and creditworthiness assessment, AI for biometric identification used in financial services, and AI used in the management of critical infrastructure. These systems are subject to Articles 13, 14, and 86 transparency and oversight requirements.

mainEntity.name: What are the penalties for non-compliance with both GDPR Article 22 and the EU AI Act?

acceptedAnswer.text: GDPR violations attract fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover. EU AI Act violations for high-risk system misuse attract up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover. Enforcement under both simultaneously is legally possible — the penalty ceilings are independent and additive.
